outage made me realise just how dependent I’ve become on email. I think I went through something resembling the five stages of grief.

Article Title: How one network change disrupted Microsoft Outlook, Teams and the AI tools that rely on them
Article Text:
The same traffic, fewer servers

Poll Vote & Share your view Would you trust Microsoft services after this incident? Yes, absolutely No, not at all 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Why the outage reached Teams, ChatGPT and Claude

Microsoft's apology and a 'promise'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A financial firm in Taiwan went back to the fax machine to confirm trades. At Europe’s Euronext exchange, email was disrupted. Shipping group Maersk warned customers that updates could take longer. The three businesses were among thousands of those caught up in a Microsoft outage that began on November 12 and took more than a day to ease. One of the world’s largest software companies had changed something in its network. A trading desk ended up reaching for a fax.Microsoft traced the outage to a problem introduced during an earlier expansion of its network capacity. The problem surfaced when the company made a subsequent network change. Microsoft ruled out a cyberattack and said AI played no role in causing the outage. Its public updates describe how servers dropped out of service, why some failed again after being restarted and how trouble in its email system reached applications well beyond Outlook. Microsoft says the Microsoft 365 outage that disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot for more than 24 hours is now fixed. In its final status update on the incident, the company said, “We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service.”The disruption hit users in at least 74 countries and left businesses, governments, hospitals and airlines falling back on phone lines, paper records and, in some offices, fax machines."I want to share what we know so far. This was not a cyberattack or an issue caused by AI tooling. Our amazing team was able to work through a very challenging situation to restore service. Our investigation points to technical challenges and failure modes (cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter) that made recovery more difficult than normal. I'm working closely with the engineering team to complete the full post-mortem. We will publish the post-mortem shortly covering the step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future. We take our responsibility to our customers seriously and will do everything we can to learn from this and prevent it going forward," wrote Charles Lamanna, EVP of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft.The failure centred on Exchange Online, the cloud service that powers Microsoft’s business email and calendars. As servers became unavailable during routine checks, the rest had to absorb their share of requests. Microsoft said total traffic had stayed steady. Engineers found that a process used to establish secure connections was getting overwhelmed on affected machines, causing them to stop responding. With less capacity available, the usual workload was enough to put the system under pressure. [ http://www.securityweek.com] That also explains why restarting servers brought only temporary relief in some cases. A machine could appear healthy after coming back online, then stop responding as it took on work. Microsoft restricted the kinds of requests some servers received while engineers tested a configuration change on a small group of machines. The company also began reversing the recent network change. It brought traffic back in stages so engineers could see whether the servers would stay up as the workload increased.Even after people could get into their inboxes, Microsoft still had to deliver the messages that had accumulated. By Friday morning in the US, the company said the backlog had shrunk substantially, though some email could still arrive late. That made recovery hard to judge from the user’s end. Outlook could open normally while a reply approving a payment, confirming a shipment or changing a meeting time was still held up. For work that depends on a timely response, the disruption lasted until the message arrived.Exchange Online also supplies data to other Microsoft products. The calendar in Teams draws on it, as do Copilot features that retrieve work email and appointments. That meant the effects varied by task. A person could still open a file stored directly in SharePoint while a feature in the same product that needed data from Exchange could fail. The list of affected products looked long because several of them called on the same underlying service.That dependency extended to rival AI assistants. Anthropic said the outage caused errors in Claude’s Microsoft 365 integration for roughly 25 hours, disrupting requests to retrieve messages, look up appointments or search for information. OpenAI reported that users could have trouble linking Microsoft services to ChatGPT and using tools that relied on those connections. Anthropic also recorded a separate problem with signing into Claude on November 13. It specifically traced the failures in its Microsoft connector and Claude for Outlook to Microsoft’s service incident.For businesses, the outage exposed how easily a second tool can run into the same problem as the first. Opening Teams to check an appointment, or asking an AI assistant to find the email it came from, can seem like two alternatives to opening Outlook. Both still need access to data held by Exchange. The Taiwanese firm’s use of a fax was a more direct workaround. It gave the firm a way to confirm trades while its usual communications were disrupted.Microsoft has promised a full incident report. Its account so far explains how the later network change triggered the outage and why restarting machines was only part of the repair. The report still has to explain what went wrong during the original upgrade and why the subsequent change could take enough servers out of service to strain those that remained. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions. Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration. We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete," the company said in a statement.The answer will help establish whether Microsoft can catch a similar problem while it is still confined to a small part of the network.
Article Summary: Microsoft traced the outage to a problem introduced during an earlier expansion of its network capacity. Microsoft ruled out a cyberattack and said AI played no role in causing the outage. The disruption hit users in at least 74 countries and left businesses, governments, hospitals and airlines falling back on phone lines, paper records and, in some offices, fax machines.

Article Title: The leather jacket comes off: How Jensen Huang lost Nvidia
Article Text:
33 years to build Nvidia, five days to lose it

Huang's affair ran straight through Nvidia's most sensitive business

Nobody at Nvidia could tell Huang no, until his own lawyer did

Once there were two affairs, the board stopped waiting for a third

Huang is out of Nvidia, but nowhere near out of the story

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Thirty-three years. That's how long Nvidia has existed, and how long Jensen Huang ran it. For most of those years, you could have sat next to him on a flight and not known who he was. Gamers knew the name on their GeForce cards, and the tech crowd knew the man behind them. Almost nobody knew that his wife, Lori, had given up her own chip design career at Silicon Graphics, where she was paid more than he was, so he could build the company.Then 2022 happened, to all of us and to Huang. Artificial intelligence stopped being a lab experiment and became the thing every government, company and investor wanted a piece of, and nearly all of them needed Nvidia's chips to get it. Huang's early bets had put him right in the middle of it, holding the one thing everybody wanted.Nvidia's chips powered the boom, and Huang made sure Nvidia's money did too. Through an investment portfolio worth about $99 billion, he struck deals with nearly every company that had anything to do with artificial intelligence, from frontier labs to cloud providers, and more than once with companies that then turned around and spent the money on Nvidia chips.Nvidia became the most valuable company on the planet. Its CEO became a celebrity who could no longer walk through a trade show without being mobbed for autographs.The black leather jacket came along for the ride. Huang had been wearing one for at least 20 years, these days picked out by Lori and their daughter, Madison, and judging by his keynotes, it makes up most of his wardrobe. Once he became famous, so did the jacket. In July, one of them sold at Sotheby's for $960,000, 16 times its high estimate, which tells you how the market was valuing anything Huang touched. Jensen Huang was now the man in the leather jacket.By December 2023, he knew Alice Huang, a former Chinese TV reporter who ran one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia.On November 8, he admitted to the affair. On November 12, he was out. The spy story alone didn't do it, because as late as November 9 his board, the president and half of Silicon Valley were still in his corner.Founders this powerful lose their companies only when they lose their boards, and by the night of November 11 Huang had handed Nvidia's directors three reasons to let him go: his affair had become a national security question about Nvidia's China business, he had built a company with no way to sideline him short of removing him, and he had broken a rule they could not look past.Plenty of CEOs have survived an affair. Plenty have not, and Huang now counts among them. Very few, though, have had one with an executive whose company was already under federal investigation for possibly smuggling their products into China.That is what set Alice Huang (no relation, before you ask) apart. Her company, Megaspeed, was set up in Singapore in 2023 and went on to buy more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips from June 2024, taking delivery of more than 200 shipments in a single year. That is a lot of hardware for a company most of the industry had never heard of. It reportedly rented that computing power to Alibaba, giving China a back door to chips Nvidia cannot sell there directly.By September 2025, the Commerce Department was investigating whether Megaspeed had helped smuggle restricted Nvidia chips into China. Nvidia kept selling to it anyway, which, for a company that prides itself on seeing years ahead, was a remarkably short-sighted call. That investigation is what led US officials to start watching Alice Huang, and to find her in contact with Huang.Their meetings were hardly cloak-and-dagger. In June 2024, after Computex, the two drank whiskey with other artificial intelligence executives at a Taipei bar, and the photo ended up on LinkedIn. A year later, local media photographed her kissing him on the cheek at a dinner in the same city.Alice Huang herself is a different story. Remarkably little is known about her, and her background is largely absent from the Chinese internet. The man she is accused of targeting has fans wearing sweaters with his face on them, while she has managed to leave barely a trace.The New York Times later reported that a memo drafted under Secretary of State Marco Rubio this spring cited intelligence that she had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to get close to Huang and nudge Nvidia toward selling its most advanced chips to China. China's embassy has called the reporting "nothing but smears against China," and she has not responded to requests for comment.Set that against Huang's last few years in Washington, where the leather jacket became a familiar sight at the White House and Lori a quiet presence beside him at state dinners.He was the industry's most persistent advocate for selling artificial intelligence chips to China, and in 2025 he talked President Donald Trump into rolling back a ban, then struck a deal that handed the US government a 25 percent cut of sales. He did draw a line at Blackwell and the upcoming Rubin. All the while, he was in a relationship with the woman officials believed was sent to influence that very argument.Trump was briefed in October 2025 and did nothing. Two months later, he approved more powerful Nvidia chip sales to China, and this May he invited Huang on a state visit to Beijing. On November 8, he said he had no regrets. "He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else," he said. Others were less relaxed. Representative Michael McCaul called it "a classic move from the CCP's playbook," and Senator Elizabeth Warren said Huang and the board "owe Congress answers. "Until that week, Huang had denied any affair. He had been brushing off questions about it internally since late 2025, and as recently as October called the relationship "all completely normal and not unusual." It took a report on November 6 that the relationship was romantic, and a visit to his house from Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, for him to finally come clean. For a CEO who has made a point of giving his executives feedback in front of everyone, he had kept this one entirely to himself.His memo on November 8 opened with Lori and their children. "I was unfaithful to my wife," he wrote. "There is no excuse for what I did." A few lines later, he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and "proud and grateful to be an American." Those are not lines a chief executive usually needs to put in an apology for an affair, and none of them could answer the question now hanging over every China decision he had touched.When a chief executive is caught in a scandal like this, there is usually a halfway step. He takes leave, a deputy runs the company for a few weeks, the board investigates, and everyone buys time.At Nvidia, that step did not exist, and Huang built it that way. He had more than 60 direct reports and a hand in every part of the business, and his son, daughter and son-in-law all worked at the company. His senior executives ran specific products and technologies, not divisions big enough to prepare anyone to run the whole thing.Succession planning came up over the years, former executives have said, and Huang resisted it. In 2023, he said he could run Nvidia for another three or four decades. For a company selling the chips behind artificial intelligence that can supposedly do almost anyone's job, Nvidia had made no plans for anyone to do Huang's.Even after Huang confessed, most of the board did not want to take a public stance, according to people familiar with the matter. It took Teter, who is also the board's secretary, to tell them they had to.So on November 8, the board opened an investigation, declared its "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team," and left him running the company while it investigated him. A spokesperson added that Huang was "committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption."That arrangement could not last, because it tied the directors' fate to his. Nvidia's 10 board members had served a combined 161 years, many of them beside Huang since the 1990s, and very little of it, by the look of things, spent saying no. A board that close to its CEO, investigating him while he still ran the show, looked less like an inquiry and more like a family meeting.By November 9, a class-action shareholder lawsuit had been filed and the stock was down about a third from its early October peak, more than $1.5 trillion in value gone. With no way to sideline him, the board was left with two options: stand behind Huang completely, or remove him completely. Huang had made sure there was no easier choice.What finally settled it had nothing to do with China.Until then, Huang's defenders had one argument that worked: he was the victim here. Trump kept making that case, calling Huang an "honorable man" who didn't know Alice Huang was a Chinese agent. Even Trump, though, had left himself some room. "I just know he's a fine person," he said, "but you never know what's going on."On November 11, The Times reported, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, that Huang had also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. In March, months after US officials had started watching his relationship with Alice Huang, Huang and Powell were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose hotel during GTC, the Nvidia conference where Huang takes the stage in his jacket every year. Powell, who is married, has not responded to requests for comment.Earlier this year, Huang had told an interviewer that Lori had been "to every conference, every speech" of his career. "Every moment of Nvidia, she was there," he said.Judging the Alice Huang affair meant weighing intelligence the board could only see in pieces. The Powell relationship needed no security clearance. Nvidia's code of conduct tells employees to steer clear of conflicts arising from "personal relationships," and many companies bar managers from relationships with people who report to them outright. For the first time, the board had a case it could decide under its own rules.It also had the start of a pattern. One relationship can be written off as a lapse. A second, surfacing within days of the first, is what makes people start looking for more, the way a couple of ants on the kitchen counter usually mean there is a whole colony behind the wall.The directors met remotely, late into the night.On November 12, Huang resigned as president, CEO and director, effective immediately. The man in the leather jacket was just Jensen Huang again.Resigned is the polite word. By the end of that meeting, Huang had been given no choice, and the man famous for his grip on every detail of Nvidia was, according to a person familiar with the situation, answering with "whatever" and "I don't care."The announcement of his ouster did not carry a single word from him, an unusual silence from a man whose keynotes routinely run past two hours. Four days earlier, he had promised employees he would "work to earn back your confidence." He never got the chance.Investors were in no mood to mourn: the shares fell another 5.5 percent that day. Within hours of the ouster, the board's caution started to look like foresight. Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had also had an intimate relationship with a second Nvidia employee, whom it did not name. Nvidia, as usual, declined to comment.Had the board kept him, it would have spent the week before earnings defending a CEO with three relationships to explain and a congressional briefing to attend. Instead, the report landed on a former chief executive.CFO Colette Kress will run the company while keeping her current job, and Harvey C. Jones becomes the first board chair in Nvidia's history. It took the company 33 years, and a scandal, to decide it needed one. Jones said he expected Nvidia's operations to "continue without interruption," the same word used four days earlier to promise that Huang was not going anywhere. Kress has called an all-hands meeting for November 18, the day after quarterly results.The search for a permanent CEO is on, and the names doing the rounds, from Kress and Nvidia's Ian Buck to Apple's Johny Srouji, AMD's Lisa Su and Arm's Rene Haas, already make a list as long as the shortlist for the next James Bond. Whoever gets the part inherits the world's most important artificial intelligence company, and possibly a few more headlines about the man who had it before. The leather jacket, mercifully, is not part of the package.Three relationships have been reported in little more than a week, and it would take a brave director to bet that the reporting stops here. Huang has also agreed to testify before Congress in the coming weeks, about Alice Huang and what she might have learnt about Nvidia's chips, and this time there will be no leather jacket to hide behind.The Commerce Department's investigation into Megaspeed is still open, and Nvidia's board has not said whether its own inquiry ends with his exit.His memo had ended with a request: "My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy." That privacy will be hard to come by. Madison and Spencer still work at Nvidia. In private, according to people who have spoken with him, Huang has taken to calling himself a "piece of sh--."His main concern now, he says, is his wife.Lori has spent four decades out of the spotlight. At an industry awards dinner in 2021, Huang walked onstage with a bottle of red wine and two glasses while she stayed in the background, as she usually did. Today she is president of the family foundation and co-trustee of a trust holding more than half of his 922 million Nvidia shares, with roughly another $5 billion of Nvidia stock in a trust she controls alone.Huang no longer runs Nvidia, and with speculation already swirling about their 41-year marriage, what happens between him and Lori may now shape his stake in the company more than anything his board decides.
Article Summary: Jensen Huang has been Nvidia's CEO for 33 years. He admitted to having an affair with a former Chinese TV reporter. The company was already under federal investigation for possibly smuggling their products into China. Huang is out of Nvidia, but nowhere near out of the story.

Article Title: Meta’s head of Infrastructure, Engineering Santosh Janardhan is leaving the company after 15 years; says in an internal memo: Time to pass ...
Article Text:
A long-time Amazon's cloud unit executive, Dave Brown joined Meta in July 2026

Meta Platforms' longtime infrastructure head will leave the company in early 2027. Santosh Janardhan, Meta’s head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, told the company's employees that he would step down from leading the infrastructure organization, according to a memo obtained by Bloomberg News. He did not detail the reasons for his departure in the message.Janardhan, who has worked at Meta since 2009, said “it’s time to pass the baton” to former AWS senior vice president David Brown , who joined Meta in July from AWS. Janardhan said in the memo that he will help support Brown through the first quarter of 2027 as part of “the transition.” He wrote, “As we make the next set of choices about our priorities, this is the right time for Dave to take the lead in shaping that work." Janardhan added in the memo, “Dave has spent his career building and operating dependable infrastructure for a wide range of demanding workloads. He has the instincts, depth and judgment this moment requires.”The announcement means that Brown will now formally lead Meta’s infrastructure efforts and serve as chief technical officer of the Meta Compute initiative, which is spearheaded by the company’s president and vice chairman Dina Powell McCormick and technical leader Daniel Gross.Dave Brown joined Meta in July 2026. Previously, he was senior vice president in Amazon Web Services. Brown joined AWS in its initial days and was a member of the early team that assembled its core EC2 service in South Africa in the 2000s. EC2, one of AWS’ oldest services, provides virtual slices of physical servers for rent, billed by the second, that companies use to run applications and websites. He was also part of Amazon CEO Andy Jassy’s S-team. Jassy's S-team is reported to be a highly influential group of 28 executives with whom CEO Jassy meets regularly to make key business decisions.According to analysts, the change of guard underscores Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s efforts to expand the company’s data center operations under newer leaders at a time of increasing investor scrutiny on capital expenditure spending by the social media giant and its hyperscaler rivals.This major leadership change comes as Meta continues to invest hundreds of billions of dollars in artificial intelligence and the data centers needed to support it.During its third quarter earnings report, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, said, "We hit major milestones this quarter toward delivering personal superintelligence for everyone - including launching Muse and Muse Wonder, our first frontier model.” It added that it expects full-year capex to fall in the range of $135 billion to $145 billion. Meta also logged negative free cash flow of $2.12 billion, which S&P Global Ratings noted as part of its decision in late October to revise Meta’s credit rating from AA- stable to AA- negative.
Article Summary: Santosh Janardhan, Meta’s head of infrastructure and co-head of engineering, told the company's employees that he would step down from leading the infrastructure organization. He did not detail the reasons for his departure in the message. Dave Brown joined Meta in July from Amazon Web Services.

Article Title: Uber, Instacart and Target can no longer charge you more based on your data in New York City; Mayor Zohran Mamdani says: New Yorkers’ personal data should never be used as a weapon against…
Article Text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

New York City Council passes law to ban surveillance pricing

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently shared a post on X (formerly Twitter) announcing a ban on “surveillance pricing” – a practice he says some companies use to charge different customers varying prices for identical goods or services. The City Council passed the legislation 44-5 on November 12, 2026, sponsored by Speaker Julie Menin with Mamdani's support; it targets data-driven price discrimination while allowing transparent loyalty programs and certain discounts. Notably, Uber , Lyft, Target, Instacart and airlines are among the companies that have faced scrutiny for alleged surveillance pricing.While many of the companies have denied using the practice, the new law seeks to prohibit it.“Some companies use your personal data, like browsing history, to serve different prices to different costumers. It’s called surveillance pricing, and we just banned it in New York City,” Mamdani wrote in the post.“This tweet will say the same thing in incognito mode, don’t worry,” he sarcastically said.The City Council on November 12 passed a bill to prohibit “surveillance pricing”. The new law bans companies from using browsing data to charge customers different prices for the same product.The surveillance pricing law passed the Democrat-dominated council in a 44-5 vote.“There are many factors that are driving up costs,” City Council Speaker Julie Menin, who sponsored the bill, said at City Hall ahead of the vote. “Some of them are quite obvious to consumers, but a more subtle reason is the insidious and predatory corporate practice of surveillance pricing.“For different consumers that are shopping at the exact same time, companies set different prices for the exact same product, taking advantage of their demographics, web browsing history, and shopping habits, as well as their social media activity, all to make New Yorkers pay more,” she added.If the companies fail to copley with the new surveillance law, they wil have to pay a fine of $1,000.
Article Summary: The City Council on November 12 passed a bill to prohibit “surveillance pricing” The new law bans companies from using browsing data to charge customers different prices for the same product. Uber, Lyft, Target, Instacart and airlines are among the companies that have faced scrutiny for alleged surveillance pricing.

Article Title: Overloaded routers and 1980s copper lines: How a network crash hit 15,000 US flights and stranded 1.5 million passengers
Article Text:
A person looks at a flight information board at LaGuardia Airport in New York, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy)

How overloaded routers on an old network forced a nationwide ground stop in the US

An update on 1980s-era copper lines appears to have crashed the system

The FAA's new SMART tool and a cyber-attack have both been ruled out for now

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Recovery will take days, and the question of backups is still open

For a little over four hours on November 13, not a single commercial flight was allowed to take off anywhere in the United States. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop just before 4pm ET after its 22 regional air traffic control centres started losing radar data and radio contact with aircraft in patches. The order was lifted at 8:15pm ET. By then, about 15,000 flights within, into or out of the US had been delayed or cancelled, according to flight tracker FlightAware, and more than 1,600 flights on November 14 were already scrapped.The fault was not on any aircraft. It sat in the FAA's telecommunications network, which moves radar data and radio traffic between the agency's facilities. When that network started passing on unreliable data, the FAA decided controllers could not safely keep planes apart. Data firm Cirium estimates around 1.5 million people were stranded. It is only the second time since 9/11 that every departure in the country has been halted.The 22 centres hit on November 13 are Air Route Traffic Control Centers. They guide planes at cruising altitude, between takeoff and landing. They rely on a constant feed of radar returns and radio links delivered over the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, a network run by defence contractor L3Harris that connects more than 4,400 FAA facilities.At 3:36pm ET, switches and routers on that network became overloaded and began passing on inconsistent data. Radar coverage dropped in and out, and controllers intermittently lost contact with some aircraft. "Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. "They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that we shut the system down. "The FAA froze departures but let the more than 3,500 planes already airborne land. Fewer than 400 were still flying by 8pm. It also extended flight plan drop times to 240 minutes at all en route centres, so filed flight plans would not time out while aircraft sat at gates. Medevac, critical cargo and law enforcement flights were exempted.Reports in the US, citing multiple sources, said an update to the network caused it to reboot, and it crashed on restart. The FAA has not confirmed this.Much of the network still runs on time-division multiplexing (TDM), an older method that sends each data stream down copper lines in fixed time slots. "We use 1980s little copper lines," Duffy said. Centres already moved to digital IP networks, which break data into packets and route them flexibly, did not fail.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the new equipment being added to the network was "overwhelming the older system". By January 2026, the FAA had replaced 40% of its copper wiring and converted 178 radio sites, so old and new hardware now run side by side on the same network.SMART, a cloud-based planning system the FAA switched on at all 22 centres on November 10, drew suspicion. It pulls together 200 data streams, but it only sends scheduling recommendations to the FAA's command centre in Warrenton, Virginia. It does not control aircraft or carry radio traffic. Air Space Intelligence, the company behind SMART, denied any role.Mullin said investigators had found "zero evidence" of a cyber-attack, with no intrusion footprints and no claims of responsibility, though he stopped short of ruling one out.The FAA restarted traffic in tiers, releasing departures as each en route centre stabilised after engineers eased the load on the overloaded switches. Airlines now have aircraft and crews out of position, and JetBlue has already warned of cancellations continuing on November 14.The last nationwide stop, on January 11, 2023, was a different kind of failure. A database error in the NOTAM system copied itself to the backup, and departures were halted for under two hours. The November 13 failure was in the network that moves the data, and it ran more than twice as long. Why backup links did not keep the centres running has not been explained.Officials put the cost of replacing the network outright at about $50 billion. Until that happens, Duffy warned, "it's going to continue to fail."
Article Summary: Not a single commercial flight was allowed to take off anywhere in the United States for four hours on November 13. The fault was not on any aircraft. It sat in the FAA's telecommunications network, which moves radar data and radio traffic between the agency's facilities.

Article Title: Microsoft denies role in FAA ground stop that caused 10,000+ flight delays and 6,600 cancellations; company says: “We have no indication that...”

Microsoft: Our outage didn’t ground US flights (Image: AP)

Microsoft has denied any link between its own global outage and the air traffic control failure that grounded every departing flight in the US on Friday. More than 10,000 flights were delayed and over 6,600 cancelled, according to flight tracker FlightAware. “We have no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services,” the company wrote on X, hours after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) froze takeoffs nationwide.The suspicion was easy to understand. Microsoft 365 had been down since Thursday, knocking out Outlook, Teams, Copilot and even Xbox Live for users in 74 countries. Then, just before 4pm ET on Friday, the FAA’s 22 regional air traffic control centres started losing radar data and radio contact with aircraft. Two massive tech failures in two days was enough for people online to connect them. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did not buy it. He told reporters they were “separate issues” and that he did not see “any reason to connect those two at all.”Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy put the blame on the FAA’s ageing network. “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data,” he said at a White House briefing, describing a system that still runs on “1980s little copper lines.”The trouble started at 3:36pm ET, and the ground stop was lifted at 8:15pm ET. Data firm Cirium estimates around 1.5 million people were stranded.Mullin said there was “zero evidence” of a cyberattack. Asked if AI was involved, he replied, “we call it SI around here,” using the administration’s preferred term for artificial intelligence.AI was an obvious suspect. Three days earlier, the FAA had switched on SMART, an AI-powered traffic planning tool from Air Space Intelligence, at all 22 centres. The company posted on X that the ground stop “is not based on or a result of the SMART system.” Duffy was blunter. “This is not even plugged in,” he said.The two failures are unrelated, but they started in similar places. Microsoft has said it is “deeply sorry” for its outage and called it “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents.” The company traced it to a flaw from an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a more recent network change.Think tank Anderson Economic Group estimates the lost productivity could cost close to $7 billion.At the FAA, reports citing people briefed on the matter say an update to the agency’s private telecom network, run by defence contractor L3Harris, made it reboot and then crash. Mullin’s account fits that picture. He said new equipment patched into the system “was overwhelming the older system.”Duffy now wants $50 billion in emergency funding from Congress to rebuild air traffic control, up from the $30 billion the administration had been seeking. “It’s going to continue to fail,” he warned.Microsoft is off the hook. The network that failed on Friday, built on copper lines older than Outlook itself, is the one carrying US flights again.
Article Summary: Microsoft and FAA outages both trace back to network changes. Article Title: Microsoft apologises and explains what is causing Outlook, Teams outage; says: 'Not related to cyber or AI'
Article Text:
Microsoft says sorry for the Outlook, Teams outage

Microsoft's full statement on the Outlook and Teams outage

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.

This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.

Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.

We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete."

How the Microsoft 365 outage went from a Teams glitch to a global email failure

Airlines, governments and AI tools among those hit by the Microsoft outage

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft has apologised for the global outage that knocked Outlook, Teams and Copilot offline for millions of users for the better part of a day. It has also finally explained what went wrong. The company says the disruption was caused by "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents." It traces the problem to an earlier network capacity upgrade, where a fault crept in and only showed itself after a more recent network change.The explanation comes nearly 24 hours after users first began reporting trouble on Thursday, around noon US Eastern time. That was close to 10:30 pm in India. Microsoft says it has fixed the underlying issue and is seeing "broad recovery and stability" across its services. Some customers and regions are still waiting for service to return, and the company has promised a full post-incident report once its review is complete.In a statement shared on social media, Microsoft said:Before the formal apology, Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said the company regretted the impact on customers who "rely on our services to get important work done every day." He added that teams were reviewing what happened and how to stop it from happening again.According to Wired, the first signs of trouble showed up around 10:40 am ET on Thursday. At that point Microsoft said it was looking into Teams issues in North America. Just before 1 pm ET, it flagged problems with Exchange Online mailboxes across the Americas. The company first pointed to "elevated load across multiple regions." It later made clear that servers were going offline, and that a surge in traffic was not to blame."We've paused all deployments. We're moving additional traffic off the affected infrastructure, and we're restarting affected servers to return them to service," Microsoft wrote at the time, Wired reported.The fix did not hold. Servers that came back online stopped responding again once traffic reached them. Meanwhile, the servers still running struggled to take on the work of the ones that had dropped out. In one update overnight, Microsoft admitted that its actions so far "have not provided the anticipated relief." Later, it described its progress on patching servers as "marginal success."That explains the slow, stage-by-stage recovery Microsoft mentions in its apology. Along the way, it also extended its email timeout window to 48 hours so that delayed messages would not bounce back. By Friday afternoon, the company said email queues were "significantly reduced and approaching normal levels." North America was recovering faster than Europe and Asia.Outage reports came in from 74 countries and territories within about an hour, according to Downdetector. Reports from India spiked at 11:21 pm local time on Thursday.In India, IndiGo said its email support services were impacted and it might not receive customer emails. Akasa Air reported delays. Air India rerouted its emails and said its flight operations were unaffected. A senior executive at a large Indian brokerage said the firm had a backup for Outlook, but client calls on Teams were a struggle. Some businesses running Zoho's workplace tools posted that their day carried on as usual.Elsewhere, Japanese government staff turned to paper copies of documents, and several UK police forces asked people to report crimes by phone. Pharmacies in Britain warned that some patients would have to wait longer for prescriptions because the health service's email system was down. A jail in Colorado could not process online bail payments because it relied on Outlook email notifications. US electric vehicle maker Workhorse Group pushed back its quarterly earnings call.OpenAI and Anthropic also reported trouble with their tools that connect to Microsoft 365.Michigan-based Anderson Economic Group estimates that lost productivity could cost close to $7 billion. It says as many as 51 million users may have had their work disrupted on Friday alone. The think tank also expects that figure to rise. Investors seem less bothered, and Microsoft shares moved only slightly when US markets opened.Security experts are asking users to stay alert as services come back. Scammers often use outages to send fake support messages that try to steal passwords or install malware. Microsoft has also warned that its Safe Links feature may not have been able to check URLs during the disruption, so links in delayed emails deserve a second look before anyone clicks them.While the outage was still going on, Wired noted that cloud failures can come from configuration errors, DNS problems or cyberattacks. Microsoft has now ruled out a cyberattack. Its post-incident report will need to explain how a flaw from an earlier upgrade went unnoticed until a later network change exposed it, and why it took the better part of a day to get millions of inboxes working again.
Article Summary: Microsoft apologises for Outlook, Teams and Copilot outage. Company says disruption was caused by "a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents" It traces the problem to an earlier network capacity upgrade, where a fault crept in and only showed itself after a recent network change.

Article Title: Vertiv launches global ecosystem for AI-scale liquid cooling infrastructure

Integrated approach to liquid cooling

Vertiv has announced a new global ecosystem initiative aimed at helping data centre operators manage and optimise liquid cooling infrastructure for AI workloads. The company said the offering combines an expanded collaboration with materials science company Dow and a new partnership with specialty chemicals and water treatment solutions provider Solenis to deliver end-to-end thermal and fluid management services. The announcement, made on November 12, comes as the rapid growth of artificial intelligence workloads drives higher computing densities in data centres, increasing the need for advanced liquid cooling systems. Vertiv said the new ecosystem brings together its infrastructure, monitoring and global service capabilities with expertise in coolant technologies, fluid chemistry and water treatment.According to Vertiv, liquid cooling is evolving beyond an equipment-level decision into a broader system management challenge. The company said system reliability and performance increasingly depend on the entire thermal chain, including heat rejection systems, chilled water infrastructure, cooling loops, coolant distribution, filtration, monitoring and controls. “AI is changing liquid cooling from an equipment decision into a system-management imperative,” said Ron Bednar, Senior Vice President of Global and Americas Services at Vertiv.“Operators need to manage thermal infrastructure, fluid health, monitoring and lifecycle service as one interconnected discipline. We believe that managing these complex interdependencies and fluid chemistry together will help operators improve system efficiency and uptime, reduce risk and extend equipment life,” he added.As part of the initiative, Vertiv has expanded its collaboration with Dow through the Dow Coolant Care Network and established a new partnership with Solenis. The companies will work together to support fluid management and thermal infrastructure services across the lifecycle of liquid-cooled environments.Vertiv said the integrated offering will enable customers to maintain fluid quality, identify system issues and optimise cooling performance through a combination of monitoring, analytics and lifecycle services.The ecosystem is designed to help operators improve compatibility across cooling systems, fluids and infrastructure components while simplifying ongoing management. Vertiv said customers will be able to use engineered flushing, commissioning, filtration and precision filling practices to maintain system cleanliness and reliability. The company also highlighted unified monitoring through its Vertiv Next Predict monitoring and analytics platform, alongside continuous monitoring and leak detection technologies aimed at identifying issues early and improving resilience.In addition, Vertiv said advanced analytics and data-driven insights will help customers optimise cooling efficiency, manage water use and proactively oversee fluid chemistry across both technical and facility water systems. The goal is to extend equipment life, improve uptime and reduce total cost of ownership for AI-scale infrastructure.Vertiv said the new ecosystem brings thermal infrastructure, fluid health, monitoring and lifecycle services together under a single operating model tailored for high-density, liquid-cooled AI deployments. The company believes this integrated approach will help operators address the increasing complexity of cooling next-generation AI data centres while maintaining performance and reliability.

The company said the offering combines an expanded collaboration with materials science company Dow and a new partnership with specialty chemicals and water treatment solutions provider Solenis.

Article Title: Microsoft 365 outage crosses 16 hours: What happens to emails you send and receive while Outlook is down, as Microsoft extends email timeout window to 48 hours
Article Text:
Outlook down: Emails get 48 hours

Microsoft has extended the email delivery window from 24 to 48 hours

Sent an email while Outlook was down: It is still on its way

When Outlook is back, your inbox may fill up all at once

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Outlook has been down for more than 16 hours for millions of Microsoft 365 users. The outage began around 11:30 pm IST on November 12, and people kept sending emails through the night without knowing where they would end up. Many are now asking the same question: what happens to all the emails sent and received while Outlook was down?Microsoft’s latest status update offers a clear answer. The company said it has extended the email timeout window to 48 hours “to protect delayed mail” while it clears the queue and backlog. Emails stuck during the outage have not vanished. They are waiting in line, and Microsoft is giving them twice the usual time to reach their destination before they are returned to the sender.Here is how email delivery normally works when something goes wrong.Exchange Online, the service that powers Outlook email for businesses, does not give up after the first failed attempt. It puts the message in a queue and tries again. Exchange retries delivery after 30 minutes initially and then every hour. The default message expiration timeout is one day. If the email still has not gone through by then, it expires and goes back to the sender as a non-delivery report, better known as a bounce message.On a normal day, 24 hours is more than enough. During an outage that has lasted most of a day, it is not. Without the change, emails sent in the first few hours of the disruption could have started bouncing back before Microsoft’s servers were ready to deliver them. The 48-hour window gives Microsoft’s recovery time to catch up.What happened to an email you sent depends on how far it travelled.If Outlook could not connect to Microsoft’s servers at all, the email most likely never left your laptop or phone. It will stay in your Outbox and send automatically once Outlook reconnects.If the email did reach Microsoft’s servers but could not be delivered, it is now part of the backlog. These are the emails the 48-hour window is meant to protect. If Microsoft delivers them within that time, the person on the other end will receive them, just late.If an email is not delivered within 48 hours, it will bounce back with the error code 4.4.7 and the words “Message expired”. That is your signal to send it again.Incoming emails follow slightly different rules, depending on who sent them.Emails from other Microsoft 365 users, such as colleagues, sit in Microsoft’s own queues. They are covered by the 48-hour window.Emails from Gmail or other services are handled by the sender’s email provider. Those servers would have kept retrying on their own schedule. The sender may have received a “delivery delayed” warning. Each provider sets its own limit, so Microsoft’s extension does not apply here. If the sender’s provider gives up first, the sender gets the bounce message, not you.Once your inbox starts working again, do not expect everything to arrive neatly. Emails are likely to land in bursts, sometimes out of order, and with timestamps from several hours earlier.Microsoft has not said how big the backlog is or how long it will take to clear. The company has only said that recovery is happening in phases and that service health “remains variable”.When Outlook is back to normal, avoid resending everything you sent during the outage. Check for bounce messages first and resend only those emails. Otherwise, recipients could end up with duplicate copies once the backlog clears. For anything urgent, a phone call is still the safer option.The 48-hour window does not fix the Microsoft 365 outage, but it does mean most emails caught in it should still reach the right inbox, as long as Microsoft restores full service before that time runs out.
Article Summary: Outlook has been down for more than 16 hours for millions of Microsoft 365 users. Microsoft has extended the email delivery window from 24 to 48 hours. If an email is not delivered within 48 hours, it will bounce back with the error code 4.4.7 and the words “Message expired”

How did fake meeting invitations trap tech workers

“sophisticated, multi-stage campaign”

FBI investigators have seized more than 900 webcam videos. The recordings belonged to tech workers targeted in a North Korean social engineering scheme called FaceStealer, which authorities said amassed more than $400 million in 18 months. The operation used fake Zoom and Teams meetings to persuade victims to install cryptocurrency-stealing malware disguised as an audio fix. Targets included cryptocurrency and web3 workers, as well as open-source developers whose access to software repositories could help hackers compromise programs used by others.According to a report by The Register, the US government said this week that a court had authorised the takedown of cloud infrastructure supporting the scheme, as part of a broader effort to disrupt North Korean cryptocurrency theft.The attacks began with invitations sent through hijacked accounts belonging to people the targets might recognise.said special agent Jeremy Robertson, who oversees counterintelligence and cyber investigations at FBI Los Angeles.he told reporters.Those addresses, designed to resemble legitimate links, opened fake meetings. Hackers secretly recorded victims while showing prerecorded footage of the supposed organiser. Some calls used deepfake videos of recognised industry figures.Robertson said.Messages told victims their audio was not working and directed them to install a software update. The download installed malware that stole cryptocurrency and sent victims’ contact lists to the attackers, helping them identify further targets. The FBI attributed FaceStealer to Sapphire Sleet, a North Korea-linked hacking group associated with Lazarus Group.Brett Leatherman, assistant director of the FBI's Cyber Division, told reporters.Separately, authorities obtained court approval to seize or restrict more than $1.2 billion linked to the October 29 Binance theft. The FBI attributed that $6.3 billion heist to TraderTraitor, another North Korean operation linked to Lazarus.Binance said preparations for thebegan in June. The attack involved fake job interviews, malware, compromised internal AI tools, control of employee devices and an “advanced transaction-authorisation method.”Investigators and private-sector partners have helped freeze more than $2.7 billion since the theft. The court authorisation covers more than $1.2 billion of those frozen assets.
Article Summary: North Korean hackers are increasingly blending cyber intrusion, social engineering, and emerging technologies such as deep fakes to make their impersonation efforts more convincing and scalable. FBI investigators have seized more than 900 webcam videos. The recordings belonged to tech workers targeted in a North Korean social engineering scheme called FaceStealer.

Article Title: Microsoft 365 outage: Outlook and Teams see improvement, company says teams are reviewing what happened
Article Text:
FILE - The logo of Microsoft is seen outside its French headquarters in Issy-les-Moulineaux, outside Paris on May 13, 2024. (AP Photo/Thibault Camus, File)

Update:

Microsoft 365 outage recovery has moved from 'marginal success' to steady progress

Outlook and Teams may still be down for some users for a while

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In a statement, Charles Lamanna, EVP, Copilot, Agents and Platform at Microsoft, said, "We are seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure. We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us. Our teams are reviewing what happened and how we can prevent similar issues going forward."Earlier on its status page, Microsoft said that recovery is now spreading across affected regions, with “broader improvements” in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe. This comes after an earlier update in which the company said recovery work had been completed across parts of its Asia Pacific infrastructure, where it is now seeing “encouraging recovery signals”. Mailbox access and delayed email processing have been improving. However, some users may still face intermittent access issues or late email deliveries while Microsoft works through the remaining affected infrastructure.It has still not shared a timeline for full restoration.The Microsoft 365 outage that has kept Outlook and Teams down for millions of users since around 11:30 pm IST on November 12 is slowly easing. More than 16 hours in, though, Microsoft is still not calling it fixed. In its latest Microsoft 365 status update, the company said recovery work has moved forward in phases across the affected infrastructure. Both its internal monitoring and customer reports, it said, point to "incremental improvement" in several services.The catch is in the second half of the same update. Microsoft said service health "remains variable" and that its systems have not fully returned to normal levels. Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 apps may work for some users and still stumble for others. The company has not shared a timeline for full restoration.The new update builds on the one Microsoft posted around 1 pm IST on November 13. That status note said the company was seeing "positive results" for server stability after applying a patch to a component that handles authentication and routing, essentially how users connect to its servers. Microsoft said then that it would expand the patch to more servers as regions came back online.The phased progress Microsoft now describes follows that patch. A little before the "positive results" note, Microsoft had reported only "marginal success" and said it was adding virtual machines to boost capacity. Hours before that, it admitted its fix was "not taking as expected".The trouble first surfaced in the Americas, where users reported they could not access their Exchange Online mailboxes. It soon spread across regions, including India. Microsoft said the problem was not a surge in traffic. Instead, a number of servers went offline unexpectedly, and the ones left running could not handle the load. Some servers that engineers revived went down again once traffic returned.Affected services include Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR. Consumer apps such as Outlook.com, OneDrive and OneNote have also been hit.For users, the phased recovery means things will not snap back for everyone at once. Some may find their Outlook inbox loading normally while a colleague still sees connection errors in Teams. Microsoft had earlier said users could see a gradual recovery as their apps reconnect to the service.In India, IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, while OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems with Microsoft connectors. Government offices in Japan switched to text messages, and the country's economy minister, Ryosei Akazawa, said the disruption had a "major impact". Article Title: Microsoft 365 outage status update: Company reports 'positive results' in fix for Outlook, Teams and other 365 services
Article Text:
Microsoft 365 outage: Fix shows results

Outlook and Teams stayed down because Microsoft's servers kept failing health checks

Microsoft says the outage is not a cyberattack

Microsoft 365 outage disrupts airlines, AI companies and governments worldwide

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft says its fix for the global Microsoft 365 outage is finally starting to work. More than 12 hours after users around the world lost access to Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services, the company said on Friday that it is seeing "positive results" for server stability. A full recovery, however, is still some way off.In its latest update on the Microsoft 365 service health page, the company said it has applied an "upstream authentication/routing configuration component patch" to a portion of its infrastructure. Put simply, the fix targets how users connect to Microsoft's servers. Microsoft said it will keep monitoring the patch and is working to roll it out to servers supporting active regions as they come back online. There is still no timeline for when services will be fully restored.The update comes shortly after Microsoft admitted it had seen only "marginal success" and was adding virtual machines to expand capacity.The trouble began around 11:30 pm IST on Thursday, when users in the Americas started reporting that they could not reach their Exchange Online mailboxes. Microsoft soon confirmed that users in any region could be affected.Impacted services include Exchange Online, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft 365 Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR. On the consumer side, Outlook.com, OneDrive, OneNote, Microsoft To Do and Microsoft 365 for the web have also seen problems.Microsoft's early updates pointed to elevated load on its infrastructure. It later clarified that traffic had not spiked. Instead, a number of servers had gone offline unexpectedly, putting pressure on the ones still running. The servers were failing automated health checks, and some that engineers brought back went unresponsive again as soon as traffic hit them. At one point, the company conceded its fix was "not taking as expected". It paused all deployments, moved traffic to other routes and blocked certain types of traffic in some regions to ease the load.Microsoft has repeatedly said there is no sign of a hack behind the disruption. "As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident," the company said in its status update. Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna also said on social media that there was "no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity".The company has promised a Post-Incident Report once the issue is resolved. It will detail the root cause and the repairs Microsoft plans to make so the same failure does not repeat.The fallout has gone well beyond office inboxes. In India, IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected. AI companies OpenAI and Anthropic reported issues with Microsoft connectors.In Japan, government email services went down, and digital minister Toshiharu Furukawa said officials would use text messages as a stopgap. Economy minister Ryosei Akazawa said the disruption had a "major impact" on the country.Australia's spy agency and federal police were among the organisations hit there, and a risk advisory firm estimated the cost to Australian businesses at billions of dollars. In the UK, several police forces asked people to call 101 instead of filing crime reports online, while schools told parents to phone in absences. Traders in Singapore and fund managers in Taiwan also fell back on phone calls and WhatsApp to confirm deals.For now, users may still have trouble connecting to Microsoft 365 apps, and recovery is likely to be gradual as clients reconnect. IT admins can follow updates under MO1550821 in the Microsoft 365 admin center, or on status.cloud.microsoft if the admin center is unavailable.The bigger question is whether the patched servers hold up once they take on full traffic. That is exactly where Microsoft's earlier attempts fell apart overnight.

A full recovery, however, is still some way off. Microsoft admitted it had seen only "marginal success" and was adding virtual machines to expand capacity.

Article Title: Nvidia employees want Jensen Huang back as CEO; internal suggestion box post draws over 1,600 comments: We are all humans and can make mistakes, Jensen did so many good things and he...

Jensen Huang may have stepped down as Nvidia CEO, but a large part of the company's workforce isn't ready to move on. An internal suggestion box post urging Nvidia's board to weigh employee sentiment before deciding Huang's future has drawn more than 1,600 comments, with most of them backing his return to the top job, according to internal correspondence reviewed by Wired.The post was written by a longtime Nvidia engineer before Huang resigned. It has since become a rallying point for staff who want the 63-year-old cofounder reinstated, despite the multiple reported extramarital affairs that led to his abrupt exit. "If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss," wrote one anonymous commenter. Another added, "We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance. "The support hasn't stayed inside the suggestion box. One employee sent an email to the entire company demanding transparency into Huang's exit. "I stand by Jensen," the staffer wrote. "Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us."The same email went a step further: "If America fails the man who helped build its future, then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang."The employee behind the email couldn't be reached for comment, while the engineer who wrote the suggestion box post declined to comment. Nvidia and its new board chair, Harvey Jones, did not immediately respond to Wired's requests for comment.Huang, who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote to employees on Sunday admitting he had been "unfaithful to [his] wife" and that there was "no excuse." The email followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.The board announced his resignation on Thursday morning, after reports of an alleged second affair, this time with a direct report. That employee has not commented on the matter. Reuters has since reported an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn't said anything about these reports since his Sunday email.The fallout has been heavy. Nvidia has lost about $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced. US lawmakers and the FBI have opened investigations, and the episode has raised the prospect of fresh export controls on chips. The board, made up largely of early Nvidia investors and Huang's longtime confidants, has named chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO. Former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones is the new chair.Work inside Nvidia has carried on as usual this week, but the resignation left many employees stunned. Within hours, about two dozen staffers posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one calling their faith in his leadership unwavering. Over the same period, Wired couldn't find a single post from an Nvidia employee supporting his exit.One employee, who has been at the company for a couple of years and wasn't authorised to speak publicly, told Wired the push for Huang's reinstatement is widespread. They worry Nvidia will suffer in the long run without its founder in charge and say the board must bring him back. "Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen," the employee said.Much of the frustration comes down to timing. Many employees expected the board's investigation to wrap up before any big changes were made. The suggestion box post had asked the board to share its findings with staff and formally gather their views "about Jensen's continuing as our CEO."That never happened. Huang stepped down just as the inquiry had begun, and staff are still looking for answers on why he left before it was done.
Article Summary: Internal post urges Nvidia board to weigh employee sentiment before deciding Huang's future. One employee sent an email to the entire company demanding transparency into Huang's exit. "If America fails the man who helped build its future, then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang," the employee wrote.

Users who are able to successfully access the Quarantine portal may encounter failures when attempting to release items from quarantine.Users may be unable to load Microsoft Defender portal pages or solution tabs.Users may encounter failures when exporting reports with sensitivity labels to PDF or PowerPoint, when updating artifacts with sensitivity labels, or opening pbix with sensitivity label in Power BI Desktop. Audit searches, protected content creation, eDiscovery tasks such as search and export, Data Classification and On Demand Scan features may also be impacted.Most of the core functionality including joining calls, meetings, group chats, and channel messages are not impacted. Scenarios that depend on Exchange Online, including Calendar related failures with scheduling, invites, viewing, and meeting edits. Creation of Live or Virtual events fail. Failures with Copilot responses for outlook, calendar, or M365 files, read history, or adding to new chats. Navigating to App chats, adding new contacts or syncing contacts in settings fail. Standard channels are working fine but users may experience the inability to create or delete private or shared channels.The app may not load, and users may see operation failures.All users may intermittently be unable to export reports with MIP sensitivity labels to PDF in Power BI.Features that depend on Exchange Online may be impacted. Accessing files stored directly in SharePoint Online remains functional.Users may encounter errors submitting print jobs or using admin features.Customers who have configured their tenant and Cloud PCs to use Microsoft Purview Customer Key for Windows 365 Cloud PCs may have users who are unable to connect to their Cloud PCs.As stated on the status page, Microsoft says it has “applied our current ongoing mitigation actions, we’ve observed a surge in outbound call volume from our routing services to our backend servers. This occurs when the backend servers outbound service cannot properly route to the backend machines”.“We’re continuing to observe heightened volume due to traffic rebalancing actions that we have taken throughout this event. We’re working on multiple workstreams to pinpoint the underlying cause of this traffic influx and address it,” the company added.Microsoft says that it will continue to monitor the effectiveness of changes applied so that refinements necessary are determined .
Article Summary: Microsoft 365 is facing a widespread outage that has disrupted access to Outlook, Teams, Microsoft Copilot and other services. Article Title: 'Servers remain stable so far': Microsoft begins restoring services after global outage hits 365 suite
Article Text:

Microsoft has begun restoring services after a widespread global outage disrupted access to its Microsoft 365 suite, including Outlook, Teams, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, SharePoint and OneDrive.The company said a portion of the affected servers had been returned to service and remained stable so far, while it was shifting traffic to alternative routes to ease the disruption."We're returning a portion of affected servers to the service, and they remain stable so far," Microsoft said in an update. It added that it had observed limited recovery after moving traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible.The company said it had also streamlined the process of bringing the remaining affected servers back online. However, it cautioned that servers restored to service could become unresponsive again once they started receiving traffic."In parallel, we're temporarily limiting which types of traffic can reach the affected infrastructure in some locations," Microsoft said.The outage affected Microsoft's email, workplace communication and cloud-based services, with nearly 130,000 users worldwide reporting problems at the peak, according to outage tracker Downdetector.Users reported difficulties accessing Outlook, sending and receiving emails and loading inboxes. Thousands also reported disruptions to Teams, Microsoft's AI assistant Copilot and other Microsoft 365 applications.Microsoft initially said it was investigating reports of users experiencing problems accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods.The company later identified elevated load across part of its infrastructure as a likely reason for the connectivity errors. It said several servers had become unexpectedly unavailable after failing automated health checks, shifting additional traffic onto the remaining infrastructure.Microsoft said the elevated load was not being caused by an overall increase in traffic, but by the reduced availability of servers.In its recovery updates, Microsoft said it had validated an alternative health-check method on a subset of affected servers, allowing them to return to service. It then began applying the fix more widely.The company also worked on an automated process to detect and restart unresponsive servers. A review of recent changes identified configuration updates as a possible cause of the disruption, although the investigation was continuing.Microsoft said it had paused deployments and configuration changes while examining whether recent updates were linked to the outage.The company also said a core process on the affected servers was becoming overwhelmed, causing them to stop responding. Earlier recovery measures had not provided the expected relief, prompting it to pursue additional ways to restore services.Microsoft had earlier reported that it had successfully restored issues affecting Teams in North America, although some users continued to experience connectivity problems, according to news agency AP.The company has not provided a definitive cause for the wider outage in the updates.Mark Gregory, an associate professor in the School of Engineering at RMIT University, told The Guardian that the disruption appeared to be affecting the network layer of Microsoft's systems.He said the unavailability of some servers could force users to rely on a smaller pool of remaining infrastructure, increasing the load on those servers and potentially causing further failures.Gregory described this as a "cascading problem" and said identifying the underlying issue, which he suggested could involve a network configuration problem, would take time.He also said companies should invest in testing environments for configuration changes before deploying them on live networks. Businesses relying on cloud services such as Microsoft 365 should maintain alternative options, he added.The outage also affected integrations connecting AI services to Microsoft's platforms. OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems with the Microsoft 365 connectors used by ChatGPT and Claude, respectively, according to The Guardian.Microsoft said customers could experience a gradual recovery as users reconnect to its services.
Article Summary: Outage affected Outlook, Teams, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, SharePoint and OneDrive. Nearly 130,000 users worldwide reported problems at the peak, according to outage tracker Downdetector. Microsoft said a portion of the affected servers had been returned to service and remained stable so far.

Article Title: Jensen Huang joins Steve Jobs, Jack Dorsey in list of tech founders who lost top jobs
Article Text:
Steve Jobs - Apple

Jack Dorsey - Twitter

Flipkart's Sachin and Binny Bansal

Jerry Yang - Yahoo

Sam Altman - Open AI

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines
